appliesToWhy: GA appendix B hand archetype `implement` lists medicine_ball_slam; one card per implement.

rightPose.text: Both hands hold the ball firmly, arms extended overhead.

gripLine.text: Hold the ball firmly with both hands, then catch it on the bounce or pick it up with both hands.

handRisks.text: A soft slam ball that does not bounce back is the safer choice.

claims.text: Hold the ball firmly with both hands.

quotes.text: Gripping the ball firming, extend your arms and bring the ball overhead.
Hold the medicine ball with both hands in front of your chest.
Hold a soft medicine ball with both hands directly in front of your torso.

claims.text: Raise the ball overhead with the arms extended before slamming it down.

quotes.text: Raise the ball overhead with extended arms.
Gripping the ball firming, extend your arms and bring the ball overhead.

claims.text: After the slam, catch the ball on the bounce if it rebounds, or pick it up with both hands.

quotes.text: Catch the ball on the bounce (if it rebounds) or pick it up quickly.
Retrieve the medicine ball with both hands and return to the starting position.
Catch the ball as it bounces back up, and bring it back up above your head.
quotes.where: How to Do Medicine Ball Slams

claims.text: A soft slam ball that does not bounce back is the safer choice, as a bouncing ball can rebound strongly off the floor.

quotes.text: a slam ball is softer and doesn’t bounce back when you slam it on the floor. Hence, the risk of injury with this ball is minimal.
Using a slam ball instead will allow you to perform the workout without fearing a strong bounce off the floor.

sources.title: How To Do Overhead Medicine Ball Slam
How to Master the Medicine Ball Slam Throw Technique

gaps: Where the hands sit on the ball (sides, top, fingers spread) not stated in any source read; only a search-engine snippet mentioned 'fingertips on the sides', not found on a page.
No coach, textbook or study source found; all sources are secondary exercise pages. PubMed search on medicine ball hand/finger injury found nothing relevant.
notes: The ACE rotational slam page (catch on rebound) is a different exercise and was not cited.
handRisks holds hand-related safety points the sources state (grip loss, over-gripping); one shared field name across the 5 implement cards.
